Its inclusion here marks its second appearance. _______________ "The whole thing was Rueldo's idea," I said, dropping my gaze to the pulsing red crystal on the table. For a moment I stared at the crystal as though I had never seen a touchglass before. Then I lifted it to my forehead and squeezed my eyes shut, as glass harp music exploded in the silent corners of my mind. For a few seconds I let the music roam caressingly through my head, easing the emptiness that filled my soul; then I set the touchglass down again. The music echoed to silence in my memory. I took a breath and slowed my heartbeat, and met the eyes of the police officers, human and pedriquat. "You've heard of Rueldo Vargas, the poet?" I said. Lieutenant Amygdol shook his head. Commander Toarn, whose furry, snouted face was framed by a pair of round velvety ears, responded by making his nose tremble. No, he whispered, he had not heard of the individual. "Oh well," I said. "He was a light, sound, and subliminal mood poet— quite well known in Landruin. A crazy old guy." "Mr. Kandrell—please," said the lieutenant. "The facts. The details of your journey." "The journey—right. Rueldo's idea entirely. I just supplied the capital and went along for the ride." "Just the two of you?" "And Arlysa Timbriun, our pilot." My voice weakened at that point, and I struggled to compose myself, to orient my memory. "Our ship was Pixikin —you know that already. We left Cervantes six weeks ago." "Your destination?" I returned Amygdol's stare. "Interstellar space. Nowhere. The void." * * * Early on in the trip, I was fascinated by everything that happened: the piloting, the engineering and navigational details, the slowly changing exterior view as Cervantes and its sun receded into the starry night. No spaceman, I had only traveled in a can twice before, on amusement rides from the moons of Aris IV. The experience was still novel and exciting, and I enjoyed listening to the faint thunder of the converters in the ship's belly driving us forward, and I liked sitting still, feeling the almost imperceptible vibration in the deck. Eventually boredom set in, and I began to spend more of my time reflecting on how I had been talked into this venture in the first place. My pride notwithstanding, I had been an easy mark for Rueldo. Not more than a few weeks before, I had skeeted in on the tachyon beam to Landruin, capital city of Cervantes—bored and lonely, and with a hundred billion stip in my pocket. I had just concluded seven years of continuous service to the Queen of Norphem, and it would be no overstatement to say that I was desperately looking for something new, preferably outlandish, to do with myself—and with my money. As a linguistic attaché to a race of giant water bugs, I had developed for myself an admirable reputation in my field, and with no place to spend my money, had accumulated a substantial bank account. I had also starved myself of the stimulation of human company for seven years, and so on my arrival in Landruin I was feeling lost, and more than a little suggestible; and when I met Rueldo at a social kazoo, I was instantly swept away by his eloquence and his visions. A month later I was in space with him, bound for . . . well, bound for empty space. Rueldo had a theory. Space, he said, had never been truly and properly explored. Oh sure, humanity and the others had roamed through a quarter of the galaxy, settling and building worlds and creating bureaucracies. But that was planets, star systems. What about space itself, which after all constituted ninety-nine point umpty-nine percent of the volume of the known universe? Hardly anyone used spaceships anymore; travelers now bypassed the tedious emptiness between the stars, in favor of the instantaneity of tachyon-beam skeeting. Some freight, of course, still went in automated barges, and there were the occasional military flights through alterspace; but those ships never lingered in the interstellar void of normalspace. "But why should they? What would anyone expect to find?" I asked, in a feisty mood, a week into the trip. Unspoken was the question. What did we expect to find? I was having trouble remembering the persuasive reasoning he had used on me earlier. Rueldo simply chuckled and poured us each a snifter of Lumion liqueur. Arlysa, though she wasn't drinking, sat down to listen. A metaxahuman from Toynbrun, she displayed all of the brooding competence for which her race was famed. Her olive-ebony complexion and severely angular facial features gave her a commanding presence. She had known Rueldo previously and appeared to trust him, but she seemed curious to hear his answer—though I don't think she cared much whether we found anything, so long as she was paid. "You're not taking me seriously," I said to Rueldo. "I take you seriously," he said. He inhaled the fumes from his liqueur. "Then answer my question." He shrugged. "I've answered it before. But, all right—the point is that space may not be as empty as everyone seems to think." "Meaning what?" I said. Interstellar space was the best vacuum this side of a Theropsid laboratory. An atom here, a molecule there, once in a great while, a dirty snowball. What else was he expecting? Rueldo glanced at Arlysa. "Do you doubt me, too?" "Elsevier's doubts are understandable," she said noncommittally. Rueldo scowled. "Oh, very well, then," he said after a moment. "Elsie, boy, there's more to this than just the fevered imagination of an old man." "I never thought—" "Yes, you did. Now shut up and let me talk." He rubbed his forehead for a moment, as Arlysa and I waited expectantly. He cleared his throat. "I've talked to you before about my astrophysical theories." "Yes," I said cautiously. That was how he had talked me into this in the first place. His theories, and his poetic visions. They now seemed pale in my memory. "Well, there's more to it than that, too. There's something personal involved—a sort of telepathic dream." He looked into his snifter, and then up again. I waited; no one rushed Rueldo when he wanted to take his time. "Imagine the following. There's a military pilot—call him Jorges—just coming in after a ten-light-year crossing. Jorges has been flying solo, with highly sensitive electronic media as cargo. The first half of the flight, everything is fine. Then, midway, his alterdrive cuts out—no warning, no reason. His ship drops into normalspace." Rueldo paused, arched his bushy eyebrows in my direction. I shrugged, and Rueldo continued. "Jorges has a total power cut-off. By the time he gets all of the trips reset and the power back on, he's nearly frozen to death. Finally he takes a moment to look out the window." "And?" Rueldo indulged me with a smile. "And he immediately questions his sanity. First he sees nothing. Blackness. But then . . ." I gestured impatiently. "Things start appearing in empty space. Shimmery things, matter forming out of the void. Hallucinatory creatures." Rueldo pursed his lips. "Do you remember the piece I had running at the Mezzo—Antics of the Night? That was my representation of the vision." I remembered. "Hell of a hallucination," I muttered. "What happened next?" Rueldo sat back in his seat, stroking the corners of his mustache. "Jorges drifts out of the zone, escapes back into alterspace and completes his journey." I looked at him questioningly, and he shrugged. "I can't tell you much more. Whatever we might see could be completely different." I felt a chill, and stared at Rueldo for a long time. "It was a hallucination. That was what you said." "I said he thought it was a hallucination. At first." Rueldo looked at me thoughtfully. "When Jorges arrived in port, his cargo was found destroyed. The media were wiped clean, all the information lost. It was no hallucination. Something was happening out there, something strange. Something, perhaps, of cosmic origin." Rueldo drained his liqueur and glanced at Arlysa. "Better watch how much you drink, old man," she said. "We're hitting alterdrive in a few hours." She pressed her lips together, and then added, "You said this was all a dream, did you not?" "It seemed in the nature of a dream," Rueldo answered. "But Jorges was quite real. When I met him, he had already encountered so much skepticism that he was rather bitter about the whole affair. Inducing him to talk required the application of certain inebriants, and the resulting state was distinctly dreamlike." Rueldo steepled his fingers, frowning in recall. "Jorges and I are telepathically compatible—and I saw and felt everything that he saw and felt in those minutes. My memory of the exchange is quite clear." I stirred uneasily. "Why didn't you tell us about this before?" Rueldo turned his head slowly, his eyes meeting mine. "I didn't want to bias your expectations, Elsie. I don't know what we're going to see." I looked at Arlysa. She arched one eyebrow, and then rose to return to the bridge. I sat with Rueldo a while longer, wondering more at my own sanity than at his. * * * We entered alterspace, and then I knew how it must feel to fall down a defective levitator shaft. In this case, we came out intact, but I had a hangover that felt worse than the real thing. Once in alterspace, however, there was nothing much for any of us to do; so Arlysa and I became better acquainted. We talked, and so on, for hours on end. Arlysa's family-group on Toynbrun was one in which romanticism was the exception, and technical and intuitive discipline the rule. As she talked, I caught glimpses of the spritely young girl she must have been, a maverick among the achievers and academics even as she learned her discipline. Though Arlysa the adult was self-reliant and reserved, there were times that a volatile passion arose in her, often when I least expected it. As for myself, I would have joyfully fallen in love. During my long tenure on the swampy world of the Norphem, I had usually had fewer than a dozen humans for company on the entire world; and that had come on the heels of my schooling years, during which I had been too busy, or too shy, to avail myself much of the pleasures of social contact. My only real relationship with a woman had come early in my school years, and the breakup of that first love had wounded my spirit for years. All things considered, you might say that I was about due. Still, I recognized Arlysa's essentially solitary ways, and—aware of my own vulnerability—I desisted from falling totally. (Ho, ho.) I tried to accept our relationship for what it was, and no more: companionship, good conversation, physical pleasure and experimentation. Much of the time we stayed apart—she with her duties and her privacy, and I with my reading and music and wiring. I asked her once whether she was carrying on with Rueldo, too—and received an answer to the effect that Rueldo preferred men, and it was none of my business anyway. Still . . . I couldn't help wondering, and feeling jealous on principle—which was stupid, I knew. Arlysa, aroused, was as attentive and demanding a partner as I could have hoped for. She loved my . . . well . . . cosmetic surgery. The part designed to look like a dragon. It was my one concession to an obsolete fashion, commissioned years ago under the influence of intoxication—an impulsiveness I was glad for now. We were in the midst of some such diversion when Pixikin dropped out of alterspace. My cabin leered at me and somersaulted, and by the time I'd recovered my equilibrium, Arlysa had already ready flown off toward the bridge, the top half of her jumpsuit fluttering behind her. I followed shakily and got to the bridge in time to hear her cursing Rueldo at the top of her lungs. "You ignorant bastard! How dare you endanger this ship! I ought to throw you overboard! I ought to let you walk home!" She paused for breath, and pulled up her jumpsuit. She closed it with an angry zip. Rueldo just glared back at her. Slowly it dawned on me that Rueldo—apparently deciding on his own that we had gone far enough—had come to the bridge and shut down the alterdrive himself. "You are a passenger!" Arlysa snarled. "P-a-s-s-e-n-g-e-r! You do not touch a control on this ship except on my orders!" "We've reached the area I want to see," he growled back. "I would have called you, but you were, how shall we say, indisposed." Arlysa finally noticed me standing behind her, and she blushed, her olive skin turning a shade darker. "That's irrelevant," she snapped. "From now on, you do not step on this bridge without my explicit permission. Now let's see what the hell you've gotten us out here for." She scowled at the instruments for a moment, then activated the viewport. The walls of the bridge dissolved, and suddenly we were standing on a ledge that jutted into the fabulous immensity of the galactic spiral arm. Stars were spattered across the heavens like a spray of molten diamond. My stomach left me, and I tottered giddily. There was nothing around me but blackness and stars and glowing gas. This view, I thought suddenly, justified the trip. We were light-years from anywhere, and the universe was playing on stage for us, and for us alone. "Damn," said Rueldo. "There's nothing here. We might have to hunt around." He dropped into a seat and folded his arms over his chest. "For now, I guess we'll just wait." Arlysa and I exchanged incredulous glances and settled into seats to wait with him. Me, I could have waited forever. * * * "Mr. Kandrell, really. Couldn't you get to the point?" Lieutenant Amygdol made a rolling gesture with his hand, and glanced at his pedriquat partner. Commander Toarn's expression was impassive, only the stirring of the fine hairs in his ears suggesting interest. "I'm trying," I said. "I have to explain—" "The disappearance of your passenger and pilot. That is what needs explaining," the lieutenant said. Commander Toarn interceded in a whisper. "Let us be patient. He will tell the story as he will. If he betrays or evades the truth, we will know." The pedriquat's eyes sharpened, and bored into mine. I swallowed, and nodded—and struggled to recapture the thread of my story. * * * Two hours later Rueldo declared that we should hop forward a tenth of a light-year. Arlysa shrugged and performed the maneuver. After another hour or so we emerged from alterspace and peered out at a view that was, to my eyes, unchanged. While Arlysa and I wondered quietly whether he had lost his marbles, Rueldo hummed and hmph'd to himself—and finally asked for another course correction, this time to the side. I wasn't sure I could take another alterspace hop without getting sick all over, but Rueldo promised that this would be the last—so I gritted my teeth and kept myself together until we dropped back into normalspace. Arlysa activated the viewport again, and the sky exploded like a holiday celebration. We were in the center of a kaleidoscope of crystalline color. The stars, stretched and distorted, rippled as I moved my head. My eyes rebelled. My stomach rose into my throat. What saved me from disgracing myself was Arlysa's outcry as the ship's power fluctuated wildly and then cut off. The controls went dark; but outside, in what should have been empty space, waves of colored light swam like living things toward the viewport. Starburst-flowers blossomed out of points of light. Whirlpools of blackness opened, devoured amber and violet streamers of light, and then imploded and vanished. The disturbance surrounded us, enclosing the ship entirely. "Elsie, get the environment units!" Arlysa yelled. While I had been staring, open mouthed, she had been struggling to restore our power. It wasn't working. The bridge was growing cold, as the ship radiated heat into space. I darted to a locker and seized three lifepacks. I tossed one to Rueldo, one to Arlysa, and strapped the third around my waist. When I flicked the switch on my own, I felt its protective shield expand slowly around me. A bit of warmth crept up my spine. The pack was working, but inefficiently; the forcefield should have snapped into place instantly. Rueldo was staring into space, holding his lifepack in his hand. I strode to his side, cinched the unit around his waist, and switched it on. A minute later, the controls flickered and slowly returned to life. "We're moving out of its influence," Arlysa muttered, her hands brushing and stabbing at the console. Outside, the swirling patterns were growing transparent; the stars shimmered and shrank to points again, tiny beacons shining through the eerie glow. "We must not leave it!" Rueldo cried, stirring from his trance. "You're mad," Arlysa said, working at the controls. "No! Go back!" I grabbed his arm. "Do you know what that thing is?" "I'm . . . beginning to," he said softly. He turned to Arlysa and strained to give his voice a commanding tone. "Take us back toward the center." "I'm taking us out," she said flatly. "Before that thing kills us. If you know what it is, start talking." Rueldo's face grew rigid with shock. "You must take us back," he whispered.
